summary: The article argues that photography and digital art festivals are driving innovation in art in late 2023 through AR, VR, and interactive installations. It covers named festivals and artists, the shift toward audience participation, and the debate over whether digital art has 'soul'. It also highlights economic and educational spillovers, sustainability benefits, and improved accessibility for artists and audiences with disabilities.
one_line: Photography and digital art festivals in late 2023 are pioneering AR/VR and interactive art while boosting local economies, sustainability, and inclusivity.
key_facts: The Imaginarium Digital Art Festival launched on September 10, 2023.
The Pixel Light Photography Expo opened on September 25.
Sophia Castellanos, creator of Imaginarium, said digital art is 'a new medium for experiencing' and that 'we're stepping into it, living it.'
Japanese artist Hiroyuki Takahashi brought his digital landscapes to life at Imaginarium using AR and VR.

Photographer Emma Richardson showed work at the Pixel Light Photography Expo where visitors experienced her images through interactive screens; her work blends traditional photography with digital manipulation.
The Luminous Flux Art and Tech Symposium started on October 3 and featured live performances with digitally augmented visuals.
Luminous Flux curator Benjamin Clarke said 'Audience participation is at the heart of innovation.'
Natalia Vargas's digital paintings were the centerpiece of the Digital Renaissance Exhibit on October 12, countering claims that digital art lacks 'soul'.
Economic analyst Jonathan Hewitt wrote that digital art festivals are becoming cornerstones of cultural innovation hubs that attract international visitors.
Host cities see spillovers in tourism and more youth engagement, and schools take field trips to the festivals to show students careers in creative technology.
Eco-artist Lila Thompson, featured at the Green Pixel Symposium on September 20, said going digital reduces the carbon footprint of art production and distribution.
Digital media offers artists with disabilities voice and motion activation and eye-tracking, while VR and AR bring experiences to audiences with mobility or sensory limits.
